questions.passage: Mara had spent three summers at the lake house, but this one felt different. Her grandmother moved more slowly now, pausing on the porch steps to catch her breath. At dinner, her grandmother kept calling Mara by her mother's name before catching herself. One afternoon, Mara found her grandmother sitting in the garden, talking softly to a rosebush as though it were an old friend. Mara sat beside her without speaking. When the sun dropped below the tree line, her grandmother patted her hand and said, 'You're a good girl, whichever one you are.'
questions.text: Which inference is best supported by evidence from the passage?
options: Mara's grandmother is angry that Mara visited so rarely
Mara's grandmother is experiencing memory difficulties
Mara dislikes spending time at the lake house
Mara's mother also visited the lake house that summer
questions.explanation: The grandmother calling Mara by her mother's name, talking to a rosebush, and saying 'whichever one you are' all provide textual evidence of memory difficulties.

questions.passage: Every year, the fishing contest drew the whole town to the pier. Old Hector always won, and the young men always swore they would beat him next time. This summer, twelve-year-old Dani entered for the first time, using a beat-up rod she had found in the garage. By noon she had caught nothing. The experienced fishers laughed and suggested she go home. Dani stayed. At dusk, she pulled in a striped bass twice the size of anything else caught that day. Hector himself shook her hand and said, 'Patience is the only tackle that matters.'
questions.text: What is the central theme of this story?
options: Fishing skill depends entirely on having the right equipment
Persistence and patience lead to success despite discouragement
Young people should not compete against experienced adults
Small towns value tradition over individual achievement
questions.explanation: Dani ignores discouragement, stays patient, and ultimately succeeds — a pattern the story reinforces with Hector's closing remark about patience.

questions.passage: At the start of the school year, Marcus refused to join any clubs. He ate lunch alone and answered teachers' questions with as few words as possible. One October afternoon, the drama teacher, Ms. Reyes, assigned Marcus the role of the narrator in the fall play — not because he auditioned, but because she heard him telling a vivid story to a stray cat in the hallway. He was furious. By opening night, however, Marcus had memorized every line and delivered them with a confidence that surprised even himself. After the final curtain, he stayed to help strike the set, chatting easily with the stagehands.
questions.text: How does Marcus change from the beginning to the end of the passage?
options: He moves from anger at Ms. Reyes to wanting to become a drama teacher himself
He shifts from isolated and withdrawn to more open and socially engaged
He transforms from a poor student into an excellent one
He changes from disliking stories to appreciating them
questions.explanation: The passage traces Marcus from deliberate isolation (eating alone, one-word answers) to chatting easily with others after the play, showing a shift in his social openness.

questions.passage: The courtroom was a glacier — slow, cold, and utterly indifferent to the people trapped within it. The judge's words fell like stones into still water, each one sending ripples through the gallery. Mireille sat at the defendant's table, her hands folded so tightly her knuckles had turned to chalk.
questions.text: In the phrase 'The courtroom was a glacier,' what does the author most likely want to convey?
options: The courtroom was located in a cold climate
The legal process was slow-moving and emotionally frigid
The judge was an unusually tall person
Mireille preferred winter weather to summer weather
questions.explanation: The metaphor comparing the courtroom to a glacier uses the glacier's qualities — slow, cold, indifferent — to characterize the legal atmosphere Mireille experiences.

questions.passage: Part One of the novel introduces Elena arriving in a new city. Part Two follows her neighbor, a retired cartographer, navigating the same city decades earlier. Part Three returns to Elena, who discovers an old hand-drawn map that matches every turn she has already taken without knowing it.
questions.text: How does the structure of the novel described above contribute to its meaning?
options: It creates suspense by withholding the ending of Elena's story until Part Three
It draws a contrast between urban and rural life across two time periods
It uses parallel timelines to suggest a hidden connection between the characters
It introduces Elena so readers have someone to follow through both storylines
questions.explanation: Placing the cartographer's past journey alongside Elena's present journey — and then connecting them through the map — creates meaning through the structural parallel.

questions.passage: The story is narrated by ten-year-old Pip, who describes his aunt as 'the tallest woman in the world and possibly the universe.' Pip reports that she once 'silenced an entire train car just by raising one eyebrow.' When the aunt herself speaks, she addresses Pip gently, asks if he has eaten, and worries aloud that he works too hard at school.
questions.text: How does the author develop the narrator's point of view in this passage?
options: By having Pip use exaggerated, admiring descriptions that reveal his awe of his aunt
By showing that Pip's aunt is genuinely the most intimidating person in the story
By contrasting Pip's immature view with the more accurate views of adult characters
By using first-person narration to show that Pip dislikes spending time with his aunt
questions.explanation: Pip's hyperbolic descriptions ('tallest woman in the universe,' silencing a train car) reflect his child's-eye admiration, which is how the author develops his subjective point of view.

questions.passage: The African elephant's trunk contains over 40,000 individual muscles, making it one of the most flexible and powerful appendages in the animal kingdom. Elephants use their trunks to breathe, smell, drink, and lift objects weighing up to 600 pounds. Researchers have also documented elephants using their trunks to comfort distressed herd members by placing them gently on another elephant's back or head. This behavior has been observed most frequently after the death of a herd member, suggesting that elephants engage in something resembling grief.
questions.text: According to the passage, what evidence supports the claim that elephants may experience grief?
options: Their trunks can lift objects weighing up to 600 pounds
They use their trunks to comfort distressed members most often after a death
Their trunks contain more than 40,000 individual muscles
Researchers have studied elephant behavior in the wild for many decades
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states that trunk-comforting behavior occurs most frequently after a herd member's death, which the author uses as evidence of grief-like behavior.

questions.passage: For centuries, maps were political documents as much as geographic ones. Cartographers working for European empires often exaggerated the size of their patrons' territories and minimized or erased the names of indigenous settlements. A blank space on a map did not mean empty land — it meant land the mapmaker chose not to acknowledge. Modern historians now read historical maps as primary sources, analyzing not just what they show but what they deliberately omit.
questions.text: What is the central idea of this passage?
options: European cartographers were less skilled than modern mapmakers
Historical maps reflect the political biases of their creators, not just geographic facts
Indigenous people rarely used maps to navigate their territories
Modern historians prefer digital maps over printed historical ones
questions.explanation: The passage argues throughout that maps were political tools shaped by their makers' interests — exaggerating territory, erasing indigenous names — not neutral geographic records.

questions.passage: In the early 1900s, most American cities lacked building codes. Landlords could construct tenement buildings with no windows in interior rooms and no fire escapes. The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire of 1911 killed 146 workers, many of whom could not escape because the exit doors had been locked from the outside. Public outrage over the disaster led directly to New York State passing 36 new labor laws within three years, including mandatory fire exits and limits on working hours. Those laws became a model for labor regulations nationwide.
questions.text: How did the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire lead to changes described in the passage?
options: It caused factory owners to voluntarily improve working conditions
It prompted public outrage that drove state legislators to pass new labor laws
It led the federal government to take over workplace safety enforcement
It showed that existing labor laws were effective but poorly enforced
questions.explanation: The passage traces a clear cause-and-effect chain: the fire caused public outrage, which led New York to pass 36 new labor laws that became a national model.

questions.passage: Unlike renewable energy sources, fossil fuels are finite — they took millions of years to form and exist in fixed quantities within the earth's crust. Once extracted and burned, they cannot be replenished on any timescale relevant to human civilization. Economists refer to this as a 'non-renewable resource constraint,' meaning that increasing consumption today reduces the supply available for future generations.
questions.text: Based on context, what does the word 'finite' most likely mean in this passage?
options: Dangerous to extract
Limited in total quantity
Difficult to locate underground
Produced by living organisms
questions.explanation: The passage explains that fossil fuels 'took millions of years to form and exist in fixed quantities' and 'cannot be replenished,' all of which point to 'finite' meaning limited in total quantity.

questions.passage: The article opens with a description of a single bee hive on a rooftop in Chicago. The second section zooms out to discuss the decline of bee populations across North America. The third section examines specific pesticides linked to colony collapse disorder. The article ends by returning to the Chicago rooftop and noting that the hive there has thrived, pesticide-free, for five years.
questions.text: Why does the author most likely return to the Chicago rooftop at the end of the article?
options: To introduce a new argument about urban farming that was not mentioned earlier
To provide a hopeful, concrete example that frames the broader problem with optimism
To argue that rooftop beekeeping is the only effective solution to colony collapse
To contrast Chicago's success with failures in other cities
questions.explanation: The structural choice of bookending the article with the same hive creates a frame that gives the broader, alarming data a hopeful conclusion through a concrete, relatable example.

questions.passage: A nutritionist writing in a health magazine argues: 'There is simply no credible scientific evidence that detox diets remove toxins from the body. The liver and kidneys perform this function continuously and effectively. Companies selling detox products are exploiting consumers' fears, not improving their health. Anyone who believes otherwise has been misled by clever marketing.'
questions.text: How would you best describe the author's point of view in this passage?
options: Cautiously optimistic that detox products may help some people
Strongly skeptical, dismissing detox diets as scientifically unsupported
Neutral, presenting both sides of the detox diet debate
Supportive of detox diets when used in moderation
questions.explanation: The author uses absolute language ('simply no credible evidence,' 'exploiting consumers') and offers no counterargument, showing a strongly skeptical point of view.

questions.passage: A student essay argues: 'Schools should start later in the morning because teenagers need more sleep. Studies show that sleep deprivation causes poor concentration. My friend Jake says he does much better on tests when he sleeps eight hours. Therefore, later school start times will improve test scores for all students.'
questions.text: Which part of this argument is weakest?
options: The claim that sleep deprivation causes poor concentration
The claim that teenagers need more sleep than younger children
Using one friend's experience as evidence for all students
The conclusion that schools should start later
questions.explanation: Citing a single friend's anecdote ('my friend Jake') as evidence for a conclusion about all students is a logical weakness — one personal example cannot support such a broad claim.

questions.text: Choose the sentence that uses pronouns in the correct case.
options: Her and Marcus walked to the library.
Marcus and she walked to the library.
Marcus and her walked to the library.
She and him walked to the library.
questions.explanation: In the subject position, subjective pronouns are required: 'she' is correct, not 'her' or 'him.' 'Marcus and she walked' is grammatically correct.

questions.text: Read this sentence: 'When students work in groups, you need to listen carefully.' What is wrong with the pronoun use?
options: The pronoun 'you' is too informal for academic writing
There is an inappropriate pronoun shift from 'students' (third person) to 'you' (second person)
The sentence needs a possessive pronoun instead of 'you'
The sentence incorrectly uses the plural 'students' with a singular pronoun
questions.explanation: The sentence begins referring to 'students' (third person plural) then shifts to 'you' (second person), creating an inconsistent pronoun shift that should be corrected to 'they need.'

questions.text: Identify the sentence with a vague pronoun reference.
options: Kenji and his brother argued until his brother finally apologized.
When Kenji argued with his brother, he finally apologized.
Kenji argued with his brother, and Kenji finally apologized.
His brother apologized to Kenji after their argument.
questions.explanation: In 'When Kenji argued with his brother, he finally apologized,' the pronoun 'he' is vague — it is unclear whether 'he' refers to Kenji or his brother.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a comma to set off a nonrestrictive element?
options: My sister who lives in Austin is a chef.
My sister, who lives in Austin, is a chef.
My sister who, lives in Austin, is a chef.
My, sister who lives in Austin, is a chef.
questions.explanation: The clause 'who lives in Austin' is nonrestrictive (it adds information but does not identify which sister) and must be set off by commas on both sides.

questions.text: Which version of this sentence uses the most varied and effective structure? Original: 'She was tired. She kept working. She finished the project.'
options: She was tired and she kept working and she finished the project.
Although she was tired, she kept working until she finished the project.
Being tired, and working, she finished.
She was tired but working finished the project.
questions.explanation: Using a subordinate clause ('Although she was tired') creates a complex sentence that shows the relationship between ideas, improving both meaning and style over the choppy originals.

questions.passage: The ancient city had been abandoned for over a thousand years. When the archaeologists arrived, they found only vestiges of the original structures — a crumbling wall here, a broken column there — suggesting that the civilization had once been far grander than its remains implied.
questions.text: Based on context, what does 'vestiges' most likely mean?
options: Complete and well-preserved ruins
Traces or remnants of something that no longer fully exists
Written records left behind by ancient people
The tools used by archaeologists in excavations
questions.explanation: The passage describes 'a crumbling wall here, a broken column there' as examples of vestiges, indicating that vestiges are remnants or traces of something once larger.

questions.text: Which sentence is an example of an oxymoron?
options: The thunderstorm roared like a lion.
She ran as fast as the wind.
The silence in the room was deafening.
Stars scattered across the sky like diamonds.
questions.explanation: An oxymoron combines two contradictory terms. 'Deafening silence' is an oxymoron — silence means no sound, while 'deafening' means extremely loud.
